extracted.intended_audience: Lords and Commons of England; Members of Parliament, policymakers, printers, writers, and the literate public concerned with press regulation
extracted.subtask_description: A 17th-century parliamentary pamphlet arguing against prior licensing of books and in favor of liberty of printing, offering prescriptive reasons and practical alternatives for regulating the press. Addresses how Parliament should treat publication, dissent, and the licensing apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose prior licensing of printed works
rubrics_metrics.description: That freedom of writing should not be restrained by a discipline imitated from the prelates and learnt by them from the Inquisition; to shut us up all again into the breast of a licenser is to give cause of doubt and discouragement to all learned and religious men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior licensing modeled on ecclesiastical or Inquisition procedures will chill learned discourse, discourage religious men from writing, and reintroduce a licenser who controls what may be said; therefore Parliament should not adopt such restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating a prelatical commission or oligarchy over the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty of printing must not be enthralled again under a prelatical commission of twenty, nullifying the people's privilege and freedom of learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not centralize control in a small body (an 'oligarchy of twenty') which would determine what the public may know; concentrated licensing power will nullify popular privilege and intellectual freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer post-publication remedies (punishment for libel) over pre-publication censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: That no book be printed, unless the printer's and the author's name, or at least the printer's, be registered; those which otherwise come forth, if they be found mischievous and libellous, the fire and the executioner will be the timeliest and the most effectual remedy that man's prevention can use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registering printers/authors and punishing libels after publication is presented as a better regulatory model than prior licensing; handle mischief by post-publication sanctions rather than preventing circulation in the first place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow public writing because it is easier to refute
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is more public than preaching; and more easy to refutation, there being so many whose business and profession merely it is to be the champions of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage open written debate: published works can be examined and refuted publicly, which is preferable to suppression or private preaching that evades public scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth thrives by exercise and free circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Our faith and knowledge thrives by exercise, as well as our limbs and complexion. Truth is compared to a streaming fountain; if her waters flow not in a perpetual progression, they sicken into a muddy pool of conformity and tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow continual discussion, disputation, and publication so truth can be exercised, developed, and corrected; curbing that flow leads to stagnation and conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship/backlash can strengthen the censured views
rubrics_metrics.description: The punishing of wits enhances their authority... a forbidden writing is thought to be a certain spark of truth that flies up in the faces of them who seek to tread it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppressing books may increase their prestige and spread; punishment can backfire by elevating the censured work and encouraging sectarian reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not suppress opinions merely for newness or unsuitableness
rubrics_metrics.description: If it be found so hurtful and so unequal to suppress opinions for the newness or the unsuitableness to a customary acceptance... I only shall repeat what I have learned from one of your own honourable number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel or unconventional opinions should not be silenced simply because they are new or offend custom; evaluate on merits rather than novelty alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerate non-fundamental differences within Christianity
rubrics_metrics.description: That neighbouring differences, or rather indifferences, are what I speak of ... which, though they may be many, yet need not interrupt THE UNITY OF SPIRIT, if we could but find among us THE BOND OF PEACE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between fundamental errors (which should be opposed) and minor doctrinal or disciplinary differences which can be tolerated to preserve unity of spirit and charitable fellowship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage debate and examination of dissenters rather than suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: If the men be erroneous who appear to be the leading schismatics... what withholds us but our sloth, our self-will, and distrust in the right cause, that we do not give them gentle meetings and gentle dismissions, that we debate not and examine the matter thoroughly with liberal and frequent audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confront and examine controversial opinions through debate, hearing, and instruction rather than stifling them by prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing will produce conformity, dull ease, and intellectual laziness
rubrics_metrics.description: There be delights, there be recreations and jolly pastimes that will fetch the day about... What need they torture their heads with that which others have taken so strictly and so unalterably into their own purveying? These are the fruits which a dull ease and cessation of our knowledge will bring forth among the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior censorship encourages passive acceptance, reducing active study and intellectual effort among clergy and laity alike; avoid measures that produce such complacency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensers are overburdened and licensing corrupts their ministry
rubrics_metrics.description: How much it hurts and hinders the licensers themselves in the calling of their ministry, more than any secular employment, if they will discharge that office as they ought, so that of necessity they must neglect either the one duty or the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning ministers the role of licensers forces them to neglect other duties and creates conflicts of vocation; the burdens of censorship can corrupt or impair offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free government nurtures intellectual vigor and invention
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the liberty, Lords and Commons, which your own valorous and happy counsels have purchased us, liberty which is the nurse of all great wits; this is that which hath rarefied and enlightened our spirits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the civil liberties that foster intellectual creativity and learning; political liberty is linked to flourishing of wit and scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let licencing be used to 'settle falsehood' and extinguish reformation
rubrics_metrics.description: It was first established and put in practice by Antichristian malice and mystery on set purpose to extinguish, if it were possible, the light of Reformation, and to settle falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of motives behind licensing schemes; they may be designed to preserve established errors and obstruct reform rather than protect truth or morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow plurality of opinions as part of building a fuller truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is much desire to learn, there of necessity will be much arguing, much writing, many opinions; for opinion in good men is but knowledge in the making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View a diversity of opinions as the productive process of knowledge formation; encourage wide discussion as evidence of a healthy search for truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free contest between Truth and Falsehood is the best test
rubrics_metrics.description: And though all the winds of doctrine were let loose to play upon the earth, so Truth be in the field, we do injuriously, by licensing and prohibiting, to misdoubt her strength. Let her and Falsehood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the worse, in a free and open encounter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow open contestation of ideas; confident truth need not be guarded by censorship because free examination will expose falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing religion to an outsourced, performative commodity
rubrics_metrics.description: A wealthy man... makes the very person of that man his religion; esteems his associating with him a sufficient evidence and commendatory of his own piety... his religion comes home at night, prays... and leaves his kind entertainer in the shop trading all day without his religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage personal engagement and ownership of religious belief rather than delegating faith entirely to a clerical 'factor' or licensed authority; civic and spiritual health requires personal exercise of conscience and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress the suppressors who would reinstate oppressive licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: If... they will persuade and execute the most Dominican part of the Inquisition over us... it would be no unequal distribution in the first place to suppress the suppressors themselves: whom the change of their condition hath puffed up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to those who would use new power to reimpose old oppressive mechanisms; resist and check actors who seek to become censors in place of the abolished prelates.
